listening.title: Maths Club Results
listening.focus: causal limits and survey bias in an after-school study
listening.script:
Maya: Have you finished the paper on the after-school maths programme at Northfield School for Dr Ellis's seminar?
Jonas: Yes, I read it last night. They tracked Year 9 students and compared exam progress for those who joined the club with those who did not, right?
Maya: That's it. The headline result looks strong. Club members improved by an average of eleven percent between January and June, while non-members improved by only four percent.
Jonas: So at first it looks like the club caused the extra progress.
Maya: Exactly, but Dr Ellis wants us to question that causal link. Participation was completely voluntary, so the two groups may have differed from the start.
Jonas: You mean self-selection? The students who signed up were probably already more interested in maths and willing to study longer.
Maya: Yes. If motivation leads both to joining and to practising at home, we cannot separate the effect of the club from the effect of motivation.
Jonas: I noted the sample was one hundred and eighty pupils in total.
Maya: Actually, I need to correct that — I misread the table earlier. It was one hundred and forty pupils, sixty in the club and eighty outside it. So the evidence base is smaller than we thought.
Jonas: Good catch. A smaller group means we should be more cautious about generalising. Did they at least match students on previous attainment?
Maya: Only partly. They paired students with similar grades last year, but they did not measure homework hours or family support. Those background factors could still explain part of the gap.
Jonas: And what about the questionnaire on study habits? I remember the response rate was not high.
Maya: Only fifty-five percent returned it, even though the researchers offered a five-pound book voucher to encourage replies. The authors note that those who replied may have been more organised than those who did not, so the habit data may be biased toward diligent students.
Jonas: So the test scores are fairly solid, but the explanation about habits is less reliable.
Maya: That's a fair summary. We can say attendance was linked to greater improvement, but we cannot claim the club alone produced it without a randomised comparison.
Jonas: Let's propose that for our presentation — run a lottery for limited club places next term and track attendance and homework time properly.

reading.title: Two Maps for One Street
reading.focus: evaluating competing flood-risk estimates and scope limits
reading.passage:
Residents of Riverton were confused last spring when two flood-risk estimates for the same riverside neighbourhood appeared within a month. Both concerned a severe flood of the River Cole, described as a one-in-one-hundred-year event, but they put very different numbers of homes at risk. The city engineering assessment listed about 300 homes. The Rivers Research Group at Midshire University listed about 520 homes. Local discussion treated the gap as proof that one side had made an error, but the reports themselves show the difference comes mainly from different questions and assumptions.
The city assessment asked how many homes would flood if the drainage upgrades completed in 2022 work as designed. It used river-gauge records from 1970 to 2020 to estimate peak water levels and combined them with a street-level model of drains and embankments. It did not add any allowance for future rainfall change, stating explicitly that its purpose was to test the current defence system under historical conditions. Its scope was therefore narrow and practical: to guide maintenance budgets for the next five years.
The university study asked a different question: how many homes could flood by 2050 if rainfall intensifies and maintenance is imperfect. It used high-resolution laser elevation data, added a fifteen percent increase in peak rainfall based on regional climate projections, and assumed thirty percent of street drains would be partly blocked by leaves and debris during autumn storms. Those two assumptions alone account for most of the extra 220 homes. The study also counted ground-floor flats in converted houses separately, while the city counted each building once.
Both reports mention the basement flooding of Riverton Library in November 2019, but they use it for different purposes. The city report cites it as an example of surface-water pooling that its upgraded drains are now designed to prevent. The university report cites the same incident as an example of how blockages can raise local water levels even when river flow is moderate. The incident itself does not prove either future estimate correct; it illustrates the mechanism each team emphasises.
The authors of this overview argue that the estimates should be read as conditional forecasts, not as competing facts about the present. Each is valid only within its stated conditions. The city figure applies if defences are fully maintained and rainfall patterns remain close to the past. The university figure applies if rainfall rises as projected and some drains are obstructed. Because neither condition can be guaranteed, neither number alone describes what will certainly happen.
For residents, the careful inference is limited. A house appearing only on the university map is not certain to flood, but it faces higher exposure under plausible future conditions with imperfect maintenance. The reports agree that comparing them directly is misleading unless assumptions about time period, drainage state, and counting method are aligned. The practical lesson is to ask what each estimate assumes before using it for insurance or planning decisions.

exercises.focus: evaluating competing flood-risk estimates and scope limits
exercises.passage:

Both concerned a severe flood of the River Cole, described as a one-in-one-hundred-year event, but they put very different numbers of homes at risk. The city report cites it as an example of surface-water pooling that its upgraded drains are now designed to prevent. The university report cites the same incident as an example of how blockages can raise local water levels even when river flow is moderate. The incident itself does not prove either future estimate correct; it illustrates the mechanism each team emphasises.
The authors of this overview argue that the estimates should be read as conditional forecasts, not as competing facts about the present. Each is valid only within its stated conditions. The reports agree that comparing them directly is misleading unless assumptions about time period, drainage state, and counting method are aligned. The practical lesson is to ask what each estimate assumes before using it for insurance or planning decisions.
exercises.prompt: What was the basis of the city engineering assessment?
options: Projected 2050 rainfall and blocked drains.
Historical gauge records from 1970 to 2020 assuming upgraded drains work as designed.
A count of insurance claims after the 2019 library flood.
Laser elevation data with separate counting of flats.
exercises.explanation: The passage states the city used 1970-2020 gauges and assumed 2022 upgrades function fully, with no climate allowance. The laser data and blocked-drain assumption belong to the university study.

The university report cites the same incident as an example of how blockages can raise local water levels even when river flow is moderate. The incident itself does not prove either future estimate correct; it illustrates the mechanism each team emphasises.
The authors of this overview argue that the estimates should be read as conditional forecasts, not as competing facts about the present. Each is valid only within its stated conditions. The city figure applies if defences are fully maintained and rainfall patterns remain close to the past. The university figure applies if rainfall rises as projected and some drains are obstructed. Because neither condition can be guaranteed, neither number alone describes what will certainly happen.
For residents, the careful inference is limited. A house appearing only on the university map is not certain to flood, but it faces higher exposure under plausible future conditions with imperfect maintenance. The reports agree that comparing them directly is misleading unless assumptions about time period, drainage state, and counting method are aligned. The practical lesson is to ask what each estimate assumes before using it for insurance or planning decisions.
exercises.prompt: What is the author's main evaluation of the two estimates?
options: The university study is factually wrong because it uses projections.
The city study is useless for maintenance planning.
Both numbers describe certain present facts and residents should average them.
They are conditional forecasts valid under different stated assumptions and should not be compared directly without alignment.
exercises.explanation: The author argues each is valid only within its conditions and direct comparison is misleading unless time period, drainage state, and counting are aligned. The averaging distractor fails because the passage warns against treating them as present facts.

writingPrompts.task: Task 1 · Reading Discovery Channels in Nortavia
writingPrompts.focus: summarising change over time and comparing groups without overstating causes
writingPrompts.prompt:
The table below shows original survey data for the fictional country of Nortavia. In both 2019 and 2024, 1,200 regular readers aged 18-65 were asked which single channel they mainly used to discover books, and how many books they completed per year on average.

Main discovery channel - Share in 2019 - Share in 2024 - Average books completed in 2019 - Average books completed in 2024:
Algorithmic recommendations (apps and websites): 22% - 41% - 7.2 books - 6.8 books
Recommendations from friends or family: 34% - 27% - 8.1 books - 8.4 books
Recommendations from librarians or bookshop staff: 26% - 15% - 9.4 books - 9.6 books
Own browsing without a recommendation: 18% - 17% - 6.5 books - 6.9 books

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Do not explain causes that are not shown by the data. Write at least 150 words in about 20 minutes.

writingPrompts.task: Task 1 · Remote and Clinic-Supported Trial Monitoring
writingPrompts.focus: comparing competing evidence and noting limits in missing data
writingPrompts.prompt:
The table below shows original fictional data from a six-month 2023 trial of a non-drug sleep routine programme called RestWell. 800 adult volunteers were divided equally into two groups: a Remote group monitored by phone app and video calls, and a Clinic group with regular in-person check-ups.

Remote group (400 starters): Completed the full 6 months: 268 participants (67%); Average missing diary days per participant: 18.4 days; Participants reporting mild issues such as morning tiredness: 42; Attended final follow-up: 61%
Clinic group (400 starters): Completed the full 6 months: 322 participants (80.5%); Average missing diary days per participant: 7.2 days; Participants reporting mild issues such as morning tiredness: 55; Attended final follow-up: 84%

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Note what the data shows and does not show about reliability. Write at least 150 words in about 20 minutes.

writingPrompts.task: Task 2 · Algorithmic Recommendations and Reading Habits
writingPrompts.focus: evaluating competing claims with attention to scope and causality
writingPrompts.prompt:
Some people argue that algorithmic recommendations from apps and websites help people discover a wider range of books, while others argue that such systems narrow reading habits by suggesting only similar titles.

Discuss both views, consider what kind of evidence could and could not prove a causal effect on habits, and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Avoid overgeneralising from single examples. Write at least 250 words in about 40 minutes.

writingPrompts.task: Task 2 · Limits of Evidence in Remote Clinical Trials
writingPrompts.focus: weighing wider inclusion against data quality and precise claims
writingPrompts.prompt:
Some people believe that remote clinical trials, in which participants take part from home using apps and video calls, should largely replace traditional clinic-based trials because they are cheaper and can include more diverse participants. Others argue that remote trials produce less complete data and should only support, not replace, in-person research.

Discuss both views and give your own opinion, paying careful attention to the limits of the evidence, such as dropout rates and missing information, and to what can reasonably be concluded about safety and effectiveness. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words in about 40 minutes.

writingPrompts.task: Task 2 · Public-Funding Trade-offs for Reading and Health
writingPrompts.prompt:
Governments have limited budgets. Some argue that public money should prioritise maintaining local libraries and community health clinics, while others argue that greater long-term benefit would come from investing the same funds in affordable high-speed internet access that supports online reading and remote health services.

Discuss both views, evaluate the trade-offs and possible unintended effects, and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Be precise about what is known and what is uncertain. Write at least 250 words in about 40 minutes.

speakingPrompts.task: Part 2 · Cue card: An Online Recommendation You Received
speakingPrompts.focus: describing an experience and evaluating its influence carefully
speakingPrompts.prompt:

speakingPrompts.task: Part 2 · Cue card: A Health Study or Trial You Heard About
speakingPrompts.focus: reporting information with awareness of evidence limits
speakingPrompts.prompt:

You have one minute to prepare and should speak for 1-2 minutes.

speakingPrompts.focus: reasoning about causality, scope and competing evidence
speakingPrompts.prompt: Discuss in more depth, giving reasons and evaluations rather than memorised facts. 1. What are the possible benefits and risks when many people rely on the same recommendation systems? 3. speakingPrompts.prompt: Answer in short, natural responses of 2-4 sentences. 1. How often do you visit a local library or community health clinic, and what do you usually do there? 2.
